stories.title: Principal Financial Group Loans $32M to Refi Queens Shopping Center
stories.excerpt: An affiliate of Mattone Investors secured $32 million to refinance Springnex Plaza, a 96,028-square-foot shopping center anchored by a Stop & Shop supermarket in the Queens neighborhood of Springfield Gardens. Principal Financial Group provided the debt, while Northmarq’s Robert Delitsky and Charles Cotsalas arranged the transaction. Delitsky noted in a statement that Mattone Investors first developed Springnex Plaza six years ago and “have done a fabulous job maintaining very strong occupancy” since then. “Supermarket-anchored shopping centers like Springnex Plaza will continue to attract very strong lender interest in today’s market,” Cotsalas added in the same statement. Located at 134-40 Springfield Boulevard, Springnex Plaza sits on 5.58 acres of land and is 100 percent occupied. Besides Stop & Shop, tenants include an IHOP, fashion retailer Ashley Stewart and Northwell Health GoHealth Urgent Care. Brian Pascus can be reached at bpascus@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Principal Financial Group refinanced 96k-sf supermarket-anchored shopping center in Queens for $32M
Springnex Plaza 100% occupied with Stop & Shop anchor; Mattone Investors owner retained asset
Lender signals strong appetite for grocery-anchored retail despite broader retail sector headwinds
stories.summary: Mattone Investors refinanced Springnex Plaza, a 96,028-square-foot supermarket-anchored shopping center in Springfield Gardens, Queens, with a $32 million loan from Principal Financial Group. The property is fully occupied with tenants including Stop & Shop, IHOP, Ashley Stewart, and a Northwell Health urgent care. Lenders continue to favor supermarket-anchored centers as a defensive, essential-use format.
stories.impact: Limited direct multifamily relevance. However, the persistent refinancing activity on stabilized retail in outer Queens—and lender confidence in essential-use anchors—suggests the submarket remains operationally sound. This signals continued economic resilience in Queens submarkets, supporting rental demand from populations serving and living near neighborhood commercial anchors.

stories.title: Data Center Development Has Domestic Materials Manufacturers Working Overtime
stories.excerpt: Development in the U.S. saw spotty progress in the first half of 2026 with costs of materials continuing to climb and asset classes with only the highest returns being built. That means data centers, power infrastructure, advanced manufacturing and pharmaceutical production are taking off, while office, retail and higher education on a national level lag way behind, due, in large part, to President Donald Trump’s ongoing tariff policies, according to a Skanska report. But just because there is a lull in some sectors does not mean supply chains for materials aren’t working at full capacity, Tom Park, vice president of national strategic supply chain at Skanska, told Commercial Observer. “The market is hot and cold right now — hot and warm may be a better way to say it — so what stands out is that we’re seeing a lot of project activity around data centers, semiconductor, life sciences,” Park said in an interview. “There’s really a lot of unprecedented demand in the mechanical, electrical, plumbing and steel space driving up lead times and cost.” Some factors causing these supply chain hemorrhages are Section 338 tariffs on Canada, delays on petrochemical import ships through the Strait of Hormuz, and domestic materials priced higher simply because of the supply and demand constraints. Tariffs on steel, aluminum and copper in particular are driving prices up. “What happens with tariffs is that it really raises the opportunity for domestic producers to raise their prices,” Park said. “For steel, aluminum and copper, the tariffs really have increased pricing on all those materials and derivative products because the foreign competition obviously has that tariff to overcome.” Lead times for material deliveries have increased from 24 to 36 weeks to 40 to 50 weeks, indicating to Park that metal mills and fabricators are running at full capacity. bullets: Trump tariff policies driving uneven U.S. development; data centers, semiconductors, life sciences accelerating
Office, retail, higher education lagging nationally due to tariff headwinds and material cost inflation
Mechanical, electrical, plumbing, steel demand at unprecedented levels; lead times and costs climbing sharply
stories.summary: First-half 2026 U.S. development saw spotty progress as tariff policies compressed activity in lower-return sectors. Data centers, semiconductors, advanced manufacturing, and pharma production are booming, while office, retail, and higher ed lag. Materials supply chains are at full capacity, pushing lead times and costs up across MEP and steel, according to Skanska's supply chain leadership.
stories.impact: Construction cost inflation on MEP and steel will raise multifamily development feasibility thresholds across all markets. Developers competing for labor and materials against data-center and life-sciences projects will face extended timelines and budget pressure. Target markets with abundant labor, local supplier capacity, and design flexibility to absorb cost increases—or pre-lock long-lead materials early in underwriting.

stories.title: Four Points Scores Refis on Two Grand Junction Rental Assets
stories.excerpt: Newmark arranged approximately $45.9 million in FHA-insured financing for two recently developed Class A multifamily communities in Grand Junction, Colorado: Nexus Apartments, a 122-unit property, and The Eddy Apartments, a 96-unit property. Newmark’s Kelley Klobetanz arranged the HUD Section 223(f) financings on behalf of the borrower, Four Points Funding, which also developed the two projects. Completed in 2024, Nexus Apartments is a market-rate multifamily community comprising a mix of walk-up apartment buildings and townhome-style residences. The property features a clubhouse, lounge, game room, community garden, barbecue area and outdoor gathering spaces. Completed in 2022, The Eddy Apartments is located along the Colorado River with Class A residences and amenities. The property offers residents direct access to the riverfront trail system connecting to Las Colonias Park, as well as amenities through a shared-use agreement with the adjacent Camp Eddy RV park, including a clubhouse, fitness center, community room and outdoor patio. bullets: Four Points Funding refinanced two recent Class A multifamily projects in Grand Junction, CO totaling $45.9M
Nexus Apartments (122 units, 2024) and The Eddy Apartments (96 units, 2022) secured HUD Section 223(f) financing

stories.summary: Newmark arranged approximately $45.9 million in HUD Section 223(f) FHA-insured financing for two recently completed Class A multifamily communities developed by Four Points Funding in Grand Junction: Nexus Apartments (122 units, completed 2024) and The Eddy Apartments (96 units, completed 2022). Both properties feature premium amenities and riverfront or walkable location positioning.
stories.impact: FHA refinancing success on recent completion indicates strong absorption and rent growth in Grand Junction multifamily. The willingness of FHA lenders to finance newly stabilized properties (within 1–2 years of completion) signals developer-friendly terms for quality product. Monitor Grand Junction demographic and employment trends; sustained FHA activity here validates the submarket as a secondary-market growth node, widening the runway for new-build acquisition and development.

stories.title: Azora, Vizcaya Capital Flip Coconut Grove Office Building for $62M
stories.excerpt: Just a year after buying a boutique office building in Miami’s coveted Coconut Grove neighborhood, Azora Private Solutions and Vizcaya Capital sold it for a nearly $15 million gain. The five-story property at 3250 Mary Street, called the Grove at 3250 Mary, sold for $62.3 million, according to the brokers who represented the sellers, Berkadia’s Omar Morales and Jaret Turkell. The joint venture had purchased the 80,000-square-foot building for $47.5 million last September. Records show the buyer is an entity tied to El-Ad National Properties, the Boca Raton-based division of Israeli billionaire Isaac Tshuva’s El-Ad Group. “Coconut Grove continues to distinguish itself as one of South Florida’s strongest real estate markets, driven by exceptional demand from luxury residential buyers and high-net-worth office users,” Morales said in a statement. “That demand, combined with limited supply, continues to attract remarkable investment to the neighborhood.” In recent years, Coconut Grove has attracted a slew of billionaires, including Google’s billionaire founder Larry Page, who spent about $170 million assembling a residential compound last year. The residential acquisitions have fueled demand for luxury office space nearby. The acquisition of the 1982-built, 1.3-acre site office building marks somewhat of a deviation for El-Ad National, which has typically focused on residential and mixed-use development. It also comes just four months after the developer purchased a nearby, low-rise condo building for $45.5 million, which will likely be redeveloped. Earlier this month, up north in Fort Lauderdale, the firm bought an oceanfront hotel for $60 million. A representative for El-Ad Group was not immediately available for comment. Julia Echikson can be reached at jechikson@commercialoserver.com.
bullets: Azora and Vizcaya Capital flipped Coconut Grove office building for $62.3M, capturing $15M gain in one year
Purchase price $47.5M (Sept 2025), sale price $62.3M (Aug 2026); buyer tied to billionaire Tshuva's El-Ad Group
Office investment thesis driven by limited supply, luxury residential demand, and high-net-worth office user demand in Coconut Grove
stories.summary: Just one year after purchasing the five-story Grove at 3250 Mary office building in Miami's Coconut Grove for $47.5 million in September 2025, Azora Private Solutions and Vizcaya Capital sold it for $62.3 million, realizing a $14.8 million gain. The buyer is an entity tied to Israeli billionaire Isaac Tshuva's El-Ad National Properties. Brokers attributed demand to luxury residential and high-net-worth office user interest, combined with constrained supply.
stories.impact: Minimal direct multifamily impact. However, the rapid appreciation and billionaire-led acquisition activity in Coconut Grove signal sustained wealth migration to South Florida and elevated land values in prime Miami neighborhoods. Monitor if such office-to-residential conversion or mixed-use repositioning opportunities emerge in Coconut Grove or adjacent submarkets, potentially unlocking value for residential developers in supply-constrained Miami micro-markets.

stories.title: NAR: Utah City Ranks Highest in U.S. for Commercial Real Estate Demand
stories.excerpt: St. George, UT ranks as the No.1 overall metro area for demand, according to the National Association of Realtors’ (NAR) inaugural Commercial Real Estate (CRE) Demand Index. The Utah city posted an overall score of 128, with multifamily as the strongest driver. The newly introduced quarterly index of 306 U.S. metro areas measures where demand is building across office, industrial, retail and multifamily sectors. Rather than measuring current property-market conditions such as vacancy rates, rents or leasing activity, the index focuses on local economic conditions that can generate demand for commercial space and provides an early view of market trends before they are reflected in traditional commercial real estate indicators such as leasing activity and vacancy rates, according to NAR. “Commercial real estate demand begins with what’s happening in the local economy,” said Nadia Evangelou, principal economist & director of real estate research at NAR. “Demand starts before a lease is signed. It starts with jobs and people. The CRE Demand Index helps identify those trends earlier, before they’re reflected in traditional market indicators.” According to the index, South Carolina ranks as the nation’s strongest state for CRE demand, reflecting continued momentum across the Carolinas. Accordingly, Raleigh, NC ranks highest among the 50 largest metro areas with a score of 121. The post NAR: Utah City Ranks Highest in U.S. for Commercial Real Estate Demand appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: St. George, UT ranks #1 nationally on NAR CRE Demand Index with overall score of 128
Multifamily identified as strongest demand driver in St. George; index measures economic conditions, not current market metrics
South Carolina ranks #1 state; index covers 306 U.S. metros and focuses on jobs, population, early leading indicators
stories.summary: St. George, Utah ranks as the nation's top metropolitan area for commercial real estate demand according to NAR's inaugural CRE Demand Index, posting a score of 128, with multifamily as the strongest sector driver. The quarterly index of 306 U.S. metros measures underlying economic conditions—job creation, population inflow, local income growth—rather than current vacancy or leasing activity, providing an early-warning tool for demand trends.
stories.impact: St. George's #1 ranking on multifamily demand signals exceptional population and job-creation fundamentals. For Trammell Crow, this warrants immediate land acquisition and feasibility assessment in St. George and surrounding Dixie County submarkets before competing developers capitalize on NAR visibility. The index's focus on leading indicators (rather than lagging metrics) means current rents and cap rates may not yet reflect the demand wave—a narrow window for advantaged pricing on development sites before the market reprices.

stories.title: W. Valley Data Center Developer Building Massive Energy System
stories.excerpt: For data centers to make their way through the permitting process, the developer most likely will have to provide power for the project without taxing current delivery systems. Copia Power is promoting a plan to do just that in Tonopah, a town about an hour west of Phoenix. The Phoenix Business Journal reports Copia Power, which develops, builds and operates grid-connected power and data center infrastructure, is working to rezone about 3,100 acres near Tonopah in the far West Valley for its latest project, the Belmont Energy Center. Most of the project site – about 2,860 acres – would be for utility-scale solar energy generation, while about 320 acres would be used for a gas generation facility, BESS and data centers. The project is backed by a $1.7 billion construction loan and has a power purchase agreement with APS. It’s expected to be operational within the next year. The post W. Valley Data Center Developer Building Massive Energy System appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Copia Power rezoning ~3,100 acres near Tonopah, AZ (west of Phoenix) for solar, gas, BESS, data centers
Belmont Energy Center backed by $1.7B construction loan; signed power purchase agreement with APS; operational within one year
2,860 acres utility-scale solar + 320 acres gas generation/BESS/data centers; infrastructure-first approach solves grid constraints for data center permitting
stories.summary: Copia Power is working to rezone approximately 3,100 acres near Tonopah, Arizona (about one hour west of Phoenix) for the Belmont Energy Center, which will include roughly 2,860 acres of utility-scale solar, 320 acres of gas generation, battery energy storage, and data center facilities. The project is backed by a $1.7 billion construction loan and a power purchase agreement with Arizona Public Service, with operations expected to begin within one year.
stories.impact: Indirect but meaningful for multifamily in greater Phoenix. The Belmont project removes grid-constraint risk for data-center and tech-cluster expansion in the far West Valley, potentially unlocking secondary population growth in Tonopah-adjacent communities. Monitor for employer announcements and residential demand along I-10 west and the Tonopah corridor; successful buildout could drive longer-term demographic shift toward West Valley, opening acquisition windows in emerging submarkets before rent and land premiums fully reflect the infrastructure-enabled growth narrative.

stories.title: Affinius Capital Lends $177M for Multifamily Asset Buy in New Jersey, Yonkers
stories.excerpt: A joint venture between Lincoln Property Company, Saber-Hightower and Waterfall Asset Management has sealed $177.25 million of acquisition financing for the purchase of two multifamily properties in the New York metropolitan area, Commercial Observer has learned. Affinus Capital provided the debt package for the sponsorship’s purchase of the 262-unit Edgewater Harbor property in Edgewater, N.J., and the soon-to-be completed 147-unit Trilogy Lofts at Tuckahoe project in Yonkers, N.Y. The deal involved a $124 million loan for Edgewater Harbor and $53.4 million of acquisition debt for Trilogy Lofts. The joint venture of Lincoln Property Company, Saber-Hightower and Waterfall Asset Management acquired both properties from National Resources as part of a $450 million acquisition of four tri-state region properties encompassing more than 4 million square feet, CO previously first reported. “Edgewater and Trilogy Lofts represent a compelling opportunity to invest in high-quality, well-located multifamily assets in supply-constrained, transit-oriented submarkets with durable renter demand,” David Greenburg, managing director at Affinius Capital, said in a statement. “Waterfall Asset Management, Lincoln Property Company and Saber-Hightower bring institutional scale, local market expertise, and a proven track record of value-add execution that positions this portfolio for long-term performance.” Cushman & Wakefield negotiated the financing with a team consisting of John Alascio, Alex Hernandez, Brad Domenico, Chuck Kohaut and Mitch Rothstein. C&W also represented the seller in the acquisition with a Northeast capital markets team of Andy Merin, Frank DiTommaso and Ryan Dowd. Located at 45 River Road 6 miles from Midtown Manhattan, Edgewater Harbor features 60,500 square feet of retail space anchored by a Sprouts Farmers Market slated to open in 2027. Pricing discipline and balance-sheet strength of larger operators (Lincoln, Saber-Hightower) are consolidating deals; independent developers should monitor financing spreads and term sheets to gauge cost of capital and underwriting standards as capital continues to favor proven sponsors with scale.

stories.title: Office CMBS Delinquencies Surpass September 2012’s All-Time High
stories.excerpt: The office CMBS delinquency rate rose to a new all-time high of 8.89% in July 2026, surpassing the previous peak of 8.83% recorded in September 2012 and up from 8.0% a year earlier, reported Fitch Ratings. Fitch’s overall U.S. CMBS delinquency rate increased 16 basis points to 3.49% in July from 3.33% in June, due primarily to new office delinquencies and the default of a large mixed-use portfolio SASB loan New 60+ day delinquency volume increased to $2.82 billion in July from $2.09 billion in June, led by office (40%, $1.12 billion), mixed-use (26%, $728 million), multifamily (14%, $405 million) and retail (10%, $274 million). Term defaults accounted for 67% ($1.88 billion) of new delinquencies, while maturity defaults represented 33%. Resolution volume declined to $1.54 billion in July from $1.63 billion in June. July resolutions included $785 million of loan liquidations, $677 million of loans brought current and $77 million of previously 60+ days delinquent loans removed from Fitch’s index after improving to 30 days delinquent. The post Office CMBS Delinquencies Surpass September 2012’s All-Time High appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Office CMBS delinquency rate hit all-time high of 8.89% in July 2026, surpassing 8.83% from September 2012
New 60+ day delinquencies reached $2.82B in July; office accounted for $1.12B (40%); multifamily $405M (14%)
Overall CMBS delinquency rate 3.49%; term defaults 67% of new delinquencies, maturity defaults 33%
stories.summary: Office CMBS delinquencies surged to an all-time high of 8.89% in July 2026, eclipsing the previous peak of 8.83% from September 2012 and up from 8.0% year-over-year. New 60+ day delinquencies totaled $2.82 billion, with office leading at $1.12 billion (40%), followed by mixed-use (26%), multifamily (14%), and retail (10%). Two-thirds of new delinquencies were term defaults; one-third maturity defaults.
stories.impact: Office stress is severe but multifamily delinquencies remain manageable at 14% of new problem volume and well-controlled in absolute dollars ($405M). This suggests multifamily credit and underwriting remain disciplined; however, rising rates and maturity defaults signal refinance headwinds ahead for 2024–2026 vintage debt. Developers should expect cap rates to compress further as fix-and-hold distressed office portfolios absorb capital flow away from higher-risk asset classes, and multifamily valuations may face downward pressure if multifamily CMBS delinquencies creep upward on maturity refinance failures later in 2026–2027.

stories.title: PGIM Loans $83M to Refi 325-Unit New Jersey Apartment Complex
stories.excerpt: The final piece to a 1,300-unit apartment portfolio refinancing has been sealed. Commercial Observer can first report that Capodagli Property Company has secured $82.6 million to refinance Meridia Roselle Park 10, a 325-unit Class A multifamily complex in Roselle, N.J. PGIM provided the debt, structured as a bridge loan, while Greystone Capital Advisors’ Drew Fletcher, Bryan Grover, Miryam Reinitz-Kops and Jesse Kopecky arranged the transaction. The deal follows $287 million in cross-collateralized bridge financing PGIM had provided for four other Class A, multifamily assets in New Jersey throughout 2025. In total, PGIM provided $369.5 million in debt for a 1,340-unit multifamily portfolio comprised of Meridia Village Commons at 209 Valley Street in South Orange, N.J.; Meridia Pompton Lakes at 61 Wanaque Avenue in Pompton Lakes, N.J.; Meridia Linden 1001 at 1001 West Elizabeth Avenue in Linden, N.J.; and Meridia Little Ferry at 110 Bergen Turnpike in Little Ferry, N.J. Meridia Roselle Park 10 is at 10 West Westfield Avenue in Roselle Park, N.J., a suburb not far from Newark Liberty International Airport and 25 miles southwest of Times Square in Manhattan. Greystone’s Fletcher said in a statement that by breaking the cross-collateralized structure into separate deals, Capodagli Property Company was able to refinance each asset “on consistent terms as each came online,” giving each deal flexibility to seek out permanent financing at its own rate. “Completing this facility reflects the strength of our long-term relationship with Capodagli and PGIM’s continued conviction in their platform,” said Fletcher. Brian Pascus can be reached at bpascus@commercialobsever.com.
bullets: PGIM provided $82.6M bridge financing to refinance Meridia Roselle Park 10 (325 units, Roselle, NJ)
Completes $369.5M cross-collateralized debt package for five-property, 1,340-unit NJ multifamily portfolio from Capodagli
All properties Class A; bridge structures indicate value-add or refinance-timing flexibility; PGIM appetite for NJ multifamily portfolio scale
stories.summary: Capodagli Property Company secured $82.6 million in bridge financing from PGIM to refinance Meridia Roselle Park 10, a 325-unit Class A multifamily complex in Roselle, New Jersey. This transaction completes a $369.5 million cross-collateralized debt package across a 1,340-unit portfolio of five Class A properties in New Jersey, including four others financed by PGIM in 2025.
stories.impact: PGIM's sustained, large-scale bridge lending to Class A multifamily portfolios in NJ signals portfolio-level refinance appetite and confidence in NJ multifamily fundamentals. Bridge structures indicate sponsorship is managing maturity or value-add timelines strategically. For developers, this validates NJ (especially North Jersey and inner Ring suburbs like Roselle Park, South Orange, Pompton Lakes) as a stable, creditor-friendly market. Monitor PGIM's willingness to extend or convert bridges—early signals of NJ market stress or credit tightening will show in refinance spreads and terms before broader cap-rate moves.
